body:
### Problem

`--api-info`/api metadata has lost all `ArrayOf` types.

Bisected the issue to https://github.com/neovim/neovim/commit/76de3e2d07f20c77b7ee6f72c8ec27b045e51ed1

### Steps to reproduce

`nvim --api-info | strings | grep -i arrayof`

### Expected behavior

Previous `ArrayOf` etc. types are present.

### Nvim version (nvim -v)

NVIM v0.12.0

### Vim (not Nvim) behaves the same?

no

### Operating system/version

Popos

### Terminal name/version

Any

### $TERM environment variable

Any

### Installation

build from repo

comment_data.body: I think this was intentional; the type has been renamed to simply `Array`.

@lewis6991 on matrix on the bisected commit:

> We wanted richer types for Lua which the PR added but needed to maintain compat for rpc types without adding the new ones. Normalizing ArrayOf to Array was the easiest route since it stood out.
> Basically it was done just to appease the tests.

Which is fair enough. Richer Lua types would eventually allow richer rpc types too.

Regarding this issue, for me this just means that I need to add few manual overrides to my API generation, which is no biggie (I should've been more proactive with my API generation as neovim progressed forward).

Before 0.12.0, I could see from `--api-info` that, e.g., `nvim_list_runtime_paths` returns an Array of `String`s such that I could generate a Swift function which returns `[String]`. Now, the `--api-info` call returns *only* `Array`, not `Array(String)` or similar. Shouldn't the API info call return that information?

> Shouldn't the API info call return that information?

Not strictly. The rpc API has a very strict contract and the fact these types ever leaked into api_info could be considered a mistake.

There is room to add these, it just needs to be formalized first.

> There is room to add these, it just needs to be formalized first.

What would that mean in practice?

> > There is room to add these, it just needs to be formalized first.
> 
> What would that mean in practice?

@justinmk

Overlaps with:

- https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/19918 
- https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/18750 

Rather than introduce a bespoke type DSL, I would suggest we do either or both of the following:

1. ship a builtin luadoc / emmylua parser so that downstream can consume `runtime/lua/vim/_meta/api.lua` and similar lua "types" files to get structured type info.
    - for convenience we can also ship a wrapper (maybe `get_api_info()` is the wrapper) so that it's easy to get a structure instead of fiddling with parser details.
2. ship existing metadata structures such as `src/nvim/eval.lua`.
    - currently we don't an equivalent file for API types, we just need to generate one from `gen_vimdoc.lua`.

How do we handle the strict contract around RPC types? Part of my pushback on #19918 is not wanting to commit to an API contract for the meta type structure as currently it is all internal and can be modified as we need to as lua annotations evolve and improve.

True. As a mitigation, I think we can unblock consumers that have a build-time generation step by providing them something in the runtime files (which may occasionally require such consumers to update their build-step), without making it part of the API contract (which is primarily intended to avoid breaking user clients).
Ok so provide an unstable utility that consumers can use but not necessarily rely on cross releases?

It's unstable in the sense that emmylua annotations are unstable; it unblocks consumers for the purpose of a build step; and it leaves the door open for a "stable" solution later.

Also, it could be "stable" if we decide to provide reified data-structures similar to `eval.lua` (i.e. [item 2](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/38734#issuecomment-4188997882)).

I strongly suggest to keep the old behavior/description for **existing** functions. This change breaks all plugins for my users that use any of the affected functions at compile time. 

> > Shouldn't the API info call return that information?
> 
> Not strictly. The rpc API has a very strict contract and the fact these types ever leaked into api_info could be considered a mistake.
> 
> There is room to add these, it just needs to be formalized first.

I really don't think that these types were unintentionally leaked. They are really useful as a consumer of a strongly typed language. And I think that the people who implemented it did a great job!

These types "leaked" for more than a decade. I haven't touched the code generation in any major way for more than a decade. Take `vim_get_windows :: forall r st. Neovim r st [Window]` as an example from [over a decade ago](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/nvim-hs-0.0.1/docs/Neovim-API-String.html
). It is a function without arguments that returns a list of `Window` values. I can pass these without any conversion to other api functions that require a window parameter. The compiler even helps me to pass it correctly. That [function still existed a year ago](https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/nvim-hs-2.3.2.4/docs/Neovim-API-String.html).

This is a silly small example, but it demonstrates my point good enough:

```haskell
queryWindowHeights :: Neovim env [Int64]
queryWindowHeights = do
    ws <- vim_get_windows
    forM ws window_get_height

-- or with some golfing:
queryWindowHeights :: Neovim env [Int64]
queryWindowHeights = vim_get_windows >>= mapM window_get_height
```

```haskell
queryWindowHeights :: Neovim env [Int64]
queryWindowHeights = do
    ws <- vim_get_windows
    forM ws (\w -> window_get_height (fromObjectUnsafe w))

-- or with some golfing:
queryWindowHeights :: Neovim env [Int64]
queryWindowHeights = vim_get_windows >>= mapM (window_get_height . fromObjectUnsafe)
```

And You might say that it's not so bad because it's just an additional function call. But as a user I now have to add a conversion that may fail. If I accidentally call `vim_get_buffers` for example, the code now compiles and fails at runtime with an error message like this:

```
Left Not the expected object: ObjectExt 0 "\STX" (Object is not convertible to: "Window" Received: ObjectExt 0 "\STX")
CallStack (from HasCallStack):
  error, called at src/Neovim/Classes.hs:127:13 in nvim-hs-2.3.2.5-inplace:Neovim.Classes
```

Before this change, I would have to write less code and receive a compiler error before I can even run the wrong program. That's fantastic!

```
    • Couldn't match type ‘Window’ with ‘Buffer’
      Expected: Buffer -> Neovim () Int64
        Actual: Window -> Neovim () Int64
    • In the first argument of ‘mapM’, namely ‘(window_get_height)’
      In the second argument of ‘(>>=)’, namely
        ‘mapM (window_get_height)’
      In the second argument of ‘($)’, namely
        ‘vim_get_buffers >>= mapM (window_get_height)’
```

And to quote the API contract:

```
As Nvim evolves the API may change in compliance with this CONTRACT:

- Function signatures will NOT CHANGE after release, except as follows:
  - Map/list parameters/results may be EXTENDED (new fields may be added).
    - Such new fields are OPTIONAL: old clients MAY ignore them.
    - Existing fields will not be removed.
  - Return type MAY CHANGE from void to non-void. Old clients MAY ignore the
    new return value.
```

This is a change to the function signatures that [breaks code in practice](https://github.com/agda/cornelis/issues/197) and therefore breaks the api contract.

I truly believe that these changes were made with good intentions, but I haven't seen a compelling argument to break the previous behavior.

> I really don't think that these types were unintentionally leaked.

It was definitely unintentional. It was never documented, and the types are based on an internal-only quasi-DSL.

The api-contract is mostly concerned with not breaking user clients. Build-time errors are much less urgent.

Anyway, this issue remains open because we haven't shut the door on it, but it will require deep thought.

> The api-contract is mostly concerned with not breaking user clients. Build-time errors are much less urgent.

This doesn't break code generation of the Neovim RPC API. This only breaks in *every* location of **client code** where such a changed function is called. This should affect most typed languages as well if they use automatic code generation for the API functions (swift was mentioned here by @qvacua).

I do have a short to mid term fix for this: I can use an older output of `nvim --api-info` to generate the code. So changing this **for my users** is not urgent.

`Object` and `ArrayOf(Object)` are really bad types in general and they are especially bad for an API. You can't really do anything with them, you have to make assumptions and hope it doesn't start breaking at some point. And these assumptions have to be made at every call site by every user.

> It was definitely unintentional. It was never documented, and the types are based on an internal-only quasi-DSL.

I'm certain that someone would have requested this "undocumented" feature 11 years ago if it wasn't there. The obvious fix for me, without looking at the technical details or knowing how much work it would be, is to just document this and restore the feature.

If this were to stay this way and I'd had to review every RPC function and possibly adjust them by hand, I don't really see the point of `nvim --api-info` then. I can just expose `nvim_call_function` in an ergonomic way and let my users do what they want. Or, if I want to spend the time, I would create a bespoke API for my language that internally only needs "nvim_call_function" and write a battery of tests. But to reiterate, what is the point of `nvim --api-info` then?

I took another look and I think I was wrong to treat this as just accidental leakage. `ArrayOf` has been present in the API metadata from the beginning, and downstream typed clients have reasonably been using it for generated bindings.

Part of what misled me was 17027d64726864c7bbdba5bee004eb581ac4b54a. That commit noted that adding the fixed-count form, e.g. `ArrayOf(Integer, 2)`, did not break clients. I read that too broadly; it does not mean clients never used the existing `ArrayOf(T)` metadata.

I've raised https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/40429 to add `ArrayOf(...)` back to exported API metadata.

It is not exactly byte-for-byte the old output: `Tuple(...)` still normalizes to `Array`, because tuple element types can be mixed. In particular, `nvim_buf_get_extmark_by_id` used to be reported as `ArrayOf(Integer)`, but that was inaccurate because the result may include the optional details dict.

> `Object` and `ArrayOf(Object)` are really bad types in general and they are especially bad for an API

That's one reason why in https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/38734#issuecomment-4188997882 I suggest aligning on the LuaLS/EmmyLua type declarations as the source of truth. Anyway, I guess we have a mitigation now.

Just FYI:

> Part of what misled me was [17027d6](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/commit/17027d64726864c7bbdba5bee004eb581ac4b54a). That commit noted that adding the fixed-count form, e.g. `ArrayOf(Integer, 2)`, did not break clients. I read that too broadly; it does not mean clients never used the existing `ArrayOf(T)` metadata.

The renaming of `Dictionary` to `Dict` was trivial to fix/support and invisible for my users, so that was fine: https://github.com/neovimhaskell/nvim-hs/commit/cfe93a70a34ccd5c106902e1ab210c415ba7b25c
I still thought it was unnecessary breakage because I didn't see any benefit in renaming it.

And from the commit message:
> The `ArrayOf(Integer, 2)` return type didn't break clients when we added
> it, which is evidence that clients don't use the `return_type` field,

In nvim-hs it was used and present since the [first release in early 2015](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/nvim-hs-0.0.1/docs/Neovim-API-String.html). The `(Int64, Int64)` tuple in the return type `window_get_position` had to use that information to generate such a type, for example. 

```haskell
window_get_position :: Window -> forall r st. Neovim r st (Either Object (Int64, Int64))
```

title: `--api-info` lost container types such as `ArrayOf`
